Area.evidence_source: Risk: Participants' descriptions of their (non)engagement with services suggested that the current organization and delivery of formal mental health care could discourage young men from access (see Figure 1). They highlighted the need for greater outreach and better advertizing, mentioning difficulties they had experienced in learning about existing services, frequently doing so only after their suicide attempt(s). Referral mechanisms and processes were perceived to further hinder access. There was a sense that if a young man did not satisfy certain predetermined criteria, he could not be referred and thus could not access services: ... Participants were acutely aware of the stigma associated with using suicide-related services. Consequently, they articulated the need for service(s) that were discrete, informal, and manifestly not associated (at least exclusively) with mental (ill) health. ... Furthermore, the young men's pervasive sense of disconnection from humanity (that "nobody cares") diminished on encountering manifestly supportive MHPs. Recovery: They highlighted the need for greater outreach and better advertizing, mentioning difficulties they had experienced in learning about existing services, frequently doing so only after their suicide attempt(s). ... For participants, these perceived barriers underscored the potential of a variety of forms of proactive outreach. Examples included educational school-based programs, enhanced media advertising (e.g., radio and television), and programs delivered in a variety of settings (e.g., youth clubs, colleges of further education). Providing outreach through mobile phone text messaging and Webbased social networking was also seen as appropriate, reflecting current patterns of interaction and communication among young people generally: ... The provision of drop-in, community-based centers, capable of affording social interaction (e.g., sports-based activities) and a generally laid-back environment, received widespread support: ... In terms of clinical care, participants emphasized the value of engaging with mental health professionals (MHPs) who were explicitly supportive. A firm interpersonal connection was achieved as a result of the MHPs not only possessing but actively communicating relevant attitudes and behaviors. These appeared to be the principal interventions that the MHPs made use of, whereby they were perceived to be present, holistically, with the young men. In this context, participants highlighted the importance of a sense of mutual respect, typically manifested by seeing themselves as being treated as an adult individual, not being talked down to: ... The development of this relationship involved additional processes that worked to establish trust. These included active listening and responding in manifestly nonjudgmental ways on the part of MHPs. ... The resultant sense of no longer being alone had a distinct countering effect on the young men's suicidal perspectives: ... The therapeutic value of such a perspective was made clear as participants described the feelings that were stimulated as a result of "their" MHP demonstrating concern. They were aware that they needed to feel that they mattered; they needed to feel that someone cared about them: ... Well, that's what helped me, knowing I had someone who actually cared.
